speaker: Andrej Karpathy
title: Skill Issue: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents, AutoResearch, and the Loopy Era of AI
question: In AI model deployment, why do frontier labs still rely on monolithic general-purpose models instead of specializing smaller models for narrow domains?
guest: Fundamentally, labs are serving a general model and don't know in advance what end users will ask about, so they have to multitask across all possible queries. You might see specialized models when partnering with a business on specific high-value niche problems, but right now labs are going after the totality of what's available. Partly, the science of manipulating model weights isn't fully developed yet—for example, fine-tuning without losing existing capabilities. We still don't have reliable primitives for customizing intelligence other than context windows. Context windows just work and are cheap to manipulate, so that's how we get customization today. Deeply adjusting a model through continual learning or domain fine-tuning means touching the weights directly, which is far trickier because you are fundamentally altering the full model and risking its general intelligence.

points.core: General-purpose API providers face unpredictable user queries requiring broad multi-domain coverage.
points.note: Accept: labs do not know what end users will ask in advance, forcing one model to multitask across all possible tasks. Do not credit: generic claims that bigger models are always smarter or better marketed.

points.core: Modifying model weights through fine-tuning risks degrading the model's broader general intelligence.
points.note: Accept: catastrophic forgetting, losing existing capabilities during fine-tuning, or lack of reliable continual-learning primitives for safe weight editing. Do not credit: vague statements that training models is expensive or takes a lot of data.

points.core: Teams customize via context windows because prompt steering avoids corrupting underlying weights.
points.note: Accept: in-context customization works reliably and cheaply compared to weight updates, making prompting the default adaptation mechanism today. Do not credit: generic mentions of RAG or prompting without contrasting it against weight-level adaptation.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The premise is only partly true: labs do ship smaller and specialized variants (distilled tiers, coding-tuned models, routing between sizes), but the flagship remains a general model for several reinforcing reasons.

First, generality itself drives capability. Training across many domains produces transfer: reasoning, world knowledge, and language skills learned broadly improve performance on narrow tasks, so large generalists often beat specialists even in the specialists' own domains. This is the "bitter lesson" pattern, where scale has repeatedly overtaken hand-tailored approaches.

Second, real tasks don't respect domain boundaries. A legal question can involve arithmetic, code, and common sense, and a narrow model fails at the edges, while routing queries to the right specialist is itself a hard, error-prone problem.

Third, economics favor one model. Training costs amortize across all use cases, and a single model is simpler to serve, evaluate, safety-test, and update than a fleet of specialists that each go stale when the next generation arrives.

Finally, customization is cheap on top of a generalist: prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and distillation deliver most of specialization's benefits without abandoning the general base.

points.why: The response explains why individual tasks can span domains but does not explain why uncertainty about future user queries requires broad coverage.
The response lists fine-tuning as a customization option without identifying the risk that weight updates can degrade existing capabilities.
The response groups prompting with fine-tuning as cheap customization without explaining why steering through context is preferable to changing weights.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Frontier labs favor monolithic general-purpose models primarily because operational economics, cross-domain reasoning, and modern serving architectures outweigh the theoretical compute savings of maintaining many narrow models. In production, serving one shared model enables high-throughput request batching, prefix caching, and uniform GPU utilization, whereas hosting dozens of specialized models fragments accelerator memory and multiplies data-curation, evaluation, safety, and maintenance overhead. Narrow specialists also require an upstream router to classify incoming prompts, adding latency and brittle failure modes whenever real-world tasks span multiple fields, such as writing Python code to audit financial contracts.

Moreover, scale unlocks positive transfer: broad training builds world knowledge and abstract reasoning skills that make generalists far more reliable than small specialists on ambiguous or out-of-distribution edge cases. Finally, frontier labs already capture many benefits of specialization inside unified deployments. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts architectures activate only a small, relevant subset of parameters per token, while long-context prompting and hot-swappable LoRA adapters tailor behavior dynamically over shared base weights—delivering domain-specific accuracy and low active inference cost without fracturing serving infrastructure.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The premise is only partly true. Frontier labs do ship specialized and smaller models, including distilled tiers like Haiku, Flash and mini, coding-tuned variants, and mixture-of-experts architectures that send each input through only part of the network. But the flagship is still a large general model, for a few reasons.

The main one is that generality transfers. Skills learned from code, math and broad text improve reasoning in other domains, so a narrow model trained from scratch usually does worse than a general model fine-tuned or prompted for the same task. Real tasks also cross domain lines: a legal question involves arithmetic, a coding task involves reading documentation. A single model avoids routing errors and the cost of maintaining many separate systems. The economics favor it too. One expensive pretraining run gets reused across thousands of uses, and smaller specialists are often cheapest to make by distilling them from the big model, which means the big model has to be built first. Finally, labs are betting that capability keeps scaling, so the frontier general model is the product, and it drives research toward broader goals like general-purpose agents.

In practice, specialization happens after training, through fine-tuning, distillation and routing, rather than replacing the general model.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Frontier labs rely on monolithic general-purpose models primarily because broad pretraining produces stronger reasoning, generalization, and robustness on edge cases than narrow specialization alone. Real-world tasks rarely stay neatly inside a single domain; a coding query may require legal, financial, or product context, and large general models transfer knowledge seamlessly across those boundaries.

Operationally, maintaining a single flagship model—or a small family of general tiers—is far simpler and cheaper to serve at scale than managing dozens of specialized models. Consolidating traffic onto one model improves GPU utilization through larger shared batches and avoids the latency, complexity, and failure modes of routing requests to the right specialist. It also amortizes the enormous cost of alignment, safety testing, and post-training across every use case. Rather than fragmenting engineering effort, labs use general models as adaptable engines steered by prompting, retrieval, and tools, reserving smaller specialized models mainly for distilled, high-volume workloads.

The response lists prompting as an adaptation method without explaining its advantage of leaving the model’s weights untouched.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Frontier labs can train one general-purpose model on a broad mix of data and reuse what it learns across many tasks. Real requests often cross domain boundaries. A single request might require reading a contract, interpreting a spreadsheet, and writing code to check the numbers. A general-purpose model can handle those steps in one context, while a collection of specialists needs a way to route the request, pass context between models, and recover when a specialist encounters something outside its domain.

There’s also an operational tradeoff. A smaller model can cost less per request and respond faster, especially for a narrow, high-volume task with clear success criteria. But each specialist adds work for training or fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment, and updates. Labs therefore often use a general-purpose model as the default or fallback and deploy smaller models where the workload is predictable and the savings justify the added complexity.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Frontier labs often use a general-purpose model because a request that looks narrow can require several skills at once. A coding assistant may need to interpret an ambiguous requirement, reason about security, and explain a trade-off. Broad training lets one model draw on all those skills, even when the developer didn’t anticipate the combination.

There’s also a deployment trade-off. A lab can spread the cost of training one strong model across many products. A fleet of specialists may be cheaper per query, but each needs suitable data, evaluation, and maintenance. The system also has to recognize which specialist can handle a request and when to fall back.

These approaches already coexist. Labs deploy smaller models when a task is stable, quality is easy to measure, and traffic is high enough for lower inference costs to justify specialization. A general-purpose model remains a practical default when requests vary or the cost of routing one incorrectly is high.
